source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

candidates.name: LLM-as-a-judge
candidates.summary: Using a language model to grade another model's outputs against criteria or a rubric. The judge may be given tools to inspect the artifact being graded, and its reliability is checked against human labels.
candidates.evidence: an agentic LLM judge that interacts with the output workbook through the same 20-tool spreadsheet environment

candidates.name: rubric-based evaluation
candidates.summary: Scoring a complex output with many fine-grained, weighted yes/no criteria written by experts. The score is the weighted share of points earned, which suits tasks that cannot be checked programmatically.
candidates.evidence: 3,225 granular rubric criteria

candidates.name: inter-annotator agreement
candidates.summary: The degree to which independent raters assign the same labels to the same items. It is used to validate annotation quality and to calibrate automated judges against human consensus.
candidates.evidence: inter-annotator alignment study over 384 binary criteria

candidates.name: Krippendorff's alpha
candidates.summary: A chance-corrected reliability coefficient for agreement among raters that handles different data types and missing ratings. A value of 1 means perfect agreement and 0 means agreement no better than chance.
candidates.evidence: we observed a Krippendorff's Alpha of 0.826

candidates.name: macro-averaged F1 score
candidates.summary: The F1 score (harmonic mean of precision and recall) computed separately for each class and then averaged with equal weight. It is used to compare classifiers, including judges against human labels.
candidates.evidence: macro-F1 score of 0.839

candidates.name: agentic evaluation harness
candidates.summary: The software environment that gives a language-model agent a set of tools, an instruction prompt and a loop for acting and observing, so that its task performance can be measured reproducibly.
candidates.evidence: an agentic harness of 20 tools organized into six categories

candidates.name: LLM agent
candidates.summary: A language model that works toward a goal over multiple steps by calling tools, reading results and deciding on further actions until it declares itself finished.
candidates.evidence: tasks LLM agents with synthesis, manipulation, and comprehension tasks

candidates.name: perturbation testing
candidates.summary: Checking that a model or program behaves correctly by changing an input, recomputing, and verifying that the dependent outputs move to the expected new values. It reveals hardcoded values and broken dependencies.
candidates.evidence: A perturbation criterion specifies an input mutation ... and an expected output shift

candidates.name: hardcoding versus formula-driven spreadsheet modeling
candidates.summary: Spreadsheets stay dynamic when cells compute from formulas that reference inputs. Typing in computed constants (hardcoding) breaks the dependency chain, so changes to inputs no longer propagate.
candidates.evidence: Do not hardcode computed values when a formula can produce the result.

candidates.name: financial modeling
candidates.summary: Building spreadsheet representations of a company's or deal's finances, linking assumptions to projected statements and valuation outputs. Standard conventions govern layout, linking and auditability.
candidates.evidence: building financial models from scratch, modifying existing models

candidates.name: discounted cash flow valuation
candidates.summary: A valuation method that projects future free cash flows and discounts them to present value at a rate such as WACC, adding a terminal value to estimate enterprise value.
candidates.evidence: building a model so I can value the company using a DCF

candidates.name: weighted average cost of capital
candidates.summary: The blended required return on a firm's debt and equity financing, weighted by their proportions and adjusted for the tax shield on debt. It serves as the discount rate in DCF valuation.
candidates.evidence: change WACC from 8.5% to 10%

candidates.name: debt schedule
candidates.summary: A model section tracking each debt tranche's balance, interest, amortization and cash sweep over time. It often creates circular references because interest depends on balances that depend on cash flow.
candidates.evidence: Build a debt schedule section at the bottom of the uploaded worksheet

candidates.name: circular reference in spreadsheets
candidates.summary: A cell formula that depends on its own result through a chain of other cells. Spreadsheets handle these with iterative calculation until values converge or fail to.
candidates.evidence: iterative-calc enabled so debt schedules and LBO-style circular references converge correctly

candidates.name: benchmark contamination
candidates.summary: The risk that evaluation items appear in a model's training data or are otherwise exposed, inflating scores. Keeping a private held-out set is a common safeguard.
candidates.evidence: We retain a private set primarily out of potential leakage concerns

candidates.name: held-out test set
candidates.summary: A portion of evaluation data not publicly released, used to measure model performance without the risk of tuning to or training on it.
candidates.evidence: held-out portion of BLUEFIN (120 tasks

candidates.name: minimal-elicitation prompting
candidates.summary: Giving a model a very short prompt without workflow prescriptions or tool preferences, so evaluation measures raw capability rather than instruction-following or prompt engineering.
candidates.evidence: we adopt a minimal-elicitation prompt (61 words

candidates.name: Pareto frontier of cost and performance
candidates.summary: The set of options for which no other option is both cheaper and better. Dominated options are those another option beats on both cost and score.
candidates.evidence: The Pareto frontier traces Grok 4.20 → Gemini 3.1 Pro → GPT-5.5

candidates.name: sandboxed code execution
candidates.summary: Running untrusted or model-generated code in a restricted environment with limited builtins, an import allow-list and timeouts, preventing file, network and system access.
candidates.evidence: restricted built-ins and a tight import whitelist (no file I/O, no network)

candidates.name: spreadsheet task taxonomy: synthesis, manipulation and interrogation
candidates.summary: A division of spreadsheet work into creating a workbook from a prompt, modifying an existing workbook, and answering questions about a workbook.
candidates.evidence: 10 end-to-end synthesis tasks ... 82 patch-based manipulation tasks ... 39 interrogation tasks

candidates.name: expert annotation and review pipeline
candidates.summary: Building a dataset by having vetted domain experts author items, then passing them through staged review and rework loops, often with AI-drafted candidate labels or rubrics that humans validate.
candidates.evidence: hundreds of domain expert hours across task creation, annotation, refinement, and review

candidates.name: programmatic verifiability
candidates.summary: Whether a task's correctness can be checked by executable tests or exact-answer matching. Benchmarks for code are often verifiable this way, while complex professional artifacts often are not.
candidates.evidence: difficult to verify programmatically but can be reliably evaluated by an LM judge

candidates.name: numeric tolerance matching
candidates.summary: Accepting a computed value as correct if it falls within a stated relative or absolute margin of a reference value, to allow for valid alternative methods and rounding.
candidates.evidence: within ±2% of $380.88

resolutions.name: LLM agent
resolutions.reason: An LLM agent that acts over multiple steps with tools is a different idea from judging model outputs or from RL training of language models.

resolutions.name: benchmark contamination
resolutions.reason: Both describe evaluation data overlapping with or leaking into training data and inflating benchmark scores, so they are synonyms.

resolutions.name: Pareto frontier of cost and performance
spreadsheet task taxonomy: synthesis, manipulation and interrogation
programmatic verifiability
resolutions.reason: Programmatic verifiability is a property of a task, while a rule-based reward is a mechanism that uses such checks, so they are related but different.
